newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Ciller blasts Europe over customs union, enlargement.
newsitem.headline: Ciller blasts Europe over customs union, enlargement.

text.p: Turkish Foreign Minister Tansu Ciller blasted the European Union on Friday, saying it had failed to honour a bilateral customs union and was unfairly shutting Ankara out of its plans to admit new members.
Ciller, who will dine with the bloc's leaders on Saturday at the Dublin summit, said the one-year-old customs union had fallen short of expectations, as associated aid had not been released.

"This first year, I have to say, has been a bit of a disappointment on the part of Turkey," Ciller told a news conference. "It's only fair that we would expect the conditions to be met by the European side."

She said that Turkey -- which on account of its poor human rights record has been left out of the EU's plans to expand eastwards -- should be the first country to be admitted, rather than being excluded.

"We have protected Europe against the threat of communism. We have protected it for a long-time as an ally of NATO. All this...makes us only a fair partner in this enlargement," she said, pointing to the fact that the customs union gave Ankara the most sophisticated trade links with the EU.
She hinted that Turkey could block the planned expansion of NATO, of which it is a member, unless the EU changes its attitude.
"You can not look at the enlargement of this institution as a separate issue -- these are interlocked institutions," she said.

Greece, which is constantly at odds with its eastern neighbour over territorial and minority rights issues, has vowed to block any moves by the EU presidency Ireland at the Dublin summit to advance relations with Ankara.
Ciller said that Greece and Turkey should sit down and hold a dialogue in a bid to sort out their many problems.
"It's about time that Turkey and Greece, Greece and Turkey sit down and talk about their differences and see which we can resolve and and what we can not," she said.
The two countries, despite being NATO allies, almost came to war earlier in the year over uninhabited islets in the Aegean Sea. The United States stepped in to broker a compromise.
Under the customs union, Ciller said, Turkey's imports from the EU have increased by more than 40 percent while its exports to the rest of the Union had increased by only seven percent.
She said that Turkey was honouring its promise to improve on human rights.

"On the human rights front we are going to work in all directions," she said, adding: "This is our dedication. This is something we are doing for our people....It's not something we are doing for our integration process."
